name: Sara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara Ziegler, 27, and I lead a three-person line crew for the electricity company. We check the switching sheet, load the truck, then spend the day fixing damaged spans and replacing worn hardware; getting a feeder back on is satisfying, but storm calls and rushed handovers wear on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work depends most on your judgment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Looking at a pole that has been repaired three times and deciding whether the drawing still matches what's in front of us. I did a two-year technical diploma, but the crew learned to trust me by watching what I do at height.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the software can tidy the outage log, but somebody still has to find the broken crossarm in the rain. My apprentice Theo will hear me say the tools are useful only when the crew can check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a quiet technology story suits me. I'm 27 and already a lead, but I know one bad call on an energized line could undo that reputation faster than any computer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the three-person repair crew and keep using the AI note tool to draft handover records. This winter I'll pay for another live-line rescue course from my training fund, then compare the practice with our current procedure before teaching Theo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, though I never feel entirely relaxed when a storm is forecast. My savings cover more than six months, and there are other utilities nearby if this firm changes its rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When does that note tool actually help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After a midnight feeder repair, it turns my rough voice notes into a readable handover before I drive home. I still check each pole number against my notebook because a neat wrong record could send the morning crew to the wrong span.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Theo about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my apprentice Theo to learn the climb and the circuit, not just the tablet. The diploma got me through the door, but the work made me worth the lead rate.

say: I'd say **field judgment** still matters when routine records get quicker.
I'd tell my crew the **AI notes** need a lineworker's check before anyone uses them.
think: I welcome a **quiet change** because my strong position survives it.
I still worry a **wrong record** could harm a crew despite tidy software.
do: Keep leading **three-person repairs** through the winter storm rota.
Check every **AI handover** against pole numbers in the notebook.
Book a **rescue course** this winter and teach Theo the procedure.
feel: **Steady**, with the usual edge of storm duty.

fieldNote: Sara uses a **notebook check** as her test of whether software helps safely.
Her **six-month cushion** and nearby utilities make a quiet future feel manageable, though storms remain a standing worry.

steps.text: Keep leading the three-person line repair crew
Check AI handovers against notebook pole numbers
Book a live-line rescue course this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let the planner use faster maps, then give the truck crew time to verify what is actually on the pole. I'd argue for paid apprenticeships if office vacancies shrink; a utility still needs people who can work safely outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our route planning and stores orders could be done with a far smaller office. My own lead pay may hold while the hands-on work remains, but faster schedules could turn each shift into a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'll ask our dispatcher Mara to show me the new routing screen and test one day's jobs against the paper switching sheet. I'll also put one extra lead-rate paycheck into savings and ask the training manager for a supervised drone inspection slot before the next storm season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about the pace, not scared of losing my van tomorrow. I like picking up tools early, but I won't sign a crew onto a timetable made by something that can't smell a hot insulator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would faster scheduling do to your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara can stack four calls on a map that look close, but traffic and a blocked access gate can eat an hour. If the supervisor treats the map as a promise, Theo is the one rushing his harness check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favor the market finding better tools; where do you draw a line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll buy a tool that saves a wasted drive. I won't accept a bonus for clearing calls faster if it makes the rescue practice the first thing cut.

say: I'd back **faster planning** if truck crews can verify field conditions.
I'd press for **paid apprenticeships** as office posts shrink.
think: I expect fewer **planning jobs** and a tighter daily schedule.
I think my **lead pay** can hold while crews still repair lines.
do: Test the **routing screen** with Mara against a paper switching sheet next month.
Save one extra **lead paycheck** before storm season.
Request a supervised **drone inspection** slot from the training manager.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed checks, though curious about useful tools.
S1.quote: I like picking up tools early, but I won't sign a crew onto a timetable made by something that can't smell a hot insulator.
fieldNote: Her support for **market tools** stops where a dispatch target could crowd out safety checks.
Sara treats **lead pay** as stable for now, yet sees the office staffing and crew schedule changing together.

steps.text: Test the AI routing screen against the switching sheet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that full thinking AI in 2028 could plan every repair, but it won't climb our poles until the robots arrive around 2031. I'd say we need honest safety trials, not a sales pitch, before any machine joins an energized crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, three years of hand work is a very short runway at 29. By 2031 I'd be 32, and a robot that can do the climb could take the premium that paid for my savings, even if a human remains to sign off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd copy my certificates and apply for the grid safety inspector opening at East Valley Utility, which is near enough to commute. If this happens, in 2029 I'll still take line shifts while shadowing its inspection crew, and I'll cap my apartment spending so I can save another two months of expenses before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one makes my stomach tighten. I have room to move and no children to feed, but the speed means even the inspector job may be temporary once thinking AI is that good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apply to inspection if thinking AI is already capable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't call inspection a safe harbor. I want the experience with faults and physical evidence, because it may give me a place in the safety trial, but I would keep applying elsewhere if those posts shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse on a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refuse a live-line trial where the robot's emergency stop sits only in a control room. I have seen a bad jumper spark at arm's length; the crew on the ground needs a stop switch.

say: I'd demand **safety trials** before capable robots work on live lines.
I'd tell crews that **2028 planning AI** still leaves field repairs until roughly 2031.
think: At **29**, I would have little time before robotic climbing arrives.
I expect my **lead premium** could shrink at 32, even if a human signs off.
do: Apply this month for the **grid inspector** opening at East Valley Utility.
Keep taking **line shifts** in 2029 while shadowing inspection crews.
Save another **two months** of expenses by capping apartment spending.
feel: **Anxious** about a short runway despite substantial savings.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be 32, and a robot that can do the climb could take the premium that paid for my savings, even if a human remains to sign off.
fieldNote: Sara understands that **inspection** can also shrink under full thinking AI; she wants experience, not a guarantee.
Her **mobility** comes from savings and nearby employers, while the three-year robot gap still feels too short for comfort.

steps.text: Apply for East Valley Utility grid safety inspector opening
Keep taking paid line shifts through 2029
Save two more months of expenses by capping apartment spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends the extra three years before thinking AI in 2031 matters, and the three after that matter even more for field crews. We should teach apprentices to question an automated switching plan before anyone lets a robot follow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 in 2031 I might still be leading repairs, but by 35 in 2034 the climbing part could go to robots. I could become the person who audits live-line trials, yet I can't count on a whole career of audit work once AI can review records too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by asking for the annual safety-audit rotation at my company, and I'd keep my line qualification current. In the first year after 2031, I'd take the paid field-verification shifts the utility still offers and apply to the regional equipment test lab for hands-on trials before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is time to build a second set of contacts, so I feel uneasy rather than cornered. It's still strange to imagine learning a trade I love just in time to supervise its replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safety-audit rotation teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend a week tracing why a recloser tripped, then write up what the site actually looked like. AI can draft that report, so I want the fault investigation and trial handling, not a desk title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay if your employer offered only shorter shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take paid verification shifts while applying to the test lab. I can afford a few months of reduced hours, but I wouldn't wait for my seniority to protect a job that has changed.

say: I'd press apprentices to **question automated** switching plans.
I'd say the **2034 robot date** gives crews a planning window.
think: By **35**, robots could take the climbing work I love.
I see **trial work** as possible, though AI could also shrink its records side.
do: Request the annual **safety-audit rotation** now and keep line qualifications current.
Apply to the **equipment test lab** for hands-on robot trials.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to build contacts but no promise of a permanent role.
S3.quote: I want the fault investigation and trial handling, not a desk title.
fieldNote: Her preferred pivot keeps **physical fault evidence** at the center rather than treating paperwork as shelter.
She would accept **reduced hours** briefly because her savings allow it, then pursue a test lab opening.

steps.text: Learn fault investigation through the annual safety-audit rotation
Apply to the regional equipment test lab

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets the utility replace equipment carefully and lets workers decide where they want to stand. I would still demand crews sign off on new climbing machines only after proper live-line tests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 when thinking AI arrives in 2036, I'd have been a lead for years; by 40 in 2039 robots might do much of my climbing. That is a real change in income, but ten years gives me a chance to earn a place testing hardware rather than chasing a desk role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd begin now by taking the manufacturer's weekend course on robotic line equipment and asking my boss to include me on equipment trials. In 2037 I'd continue paid field work, put my trial log in applications to two nearby utilities, and keep saving a set part of each lead paycheck before the 2039 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture a future here without pretending today's job lasts forever. The long warning makes me calmer, though I'll miss the feeling of fixing a line with my own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in that trial log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record where a gripper slips on old hardware, what the crew did to make it safe, and whether the fix held in rain. A glossy demonstration won't show that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young apprentice joining in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new apprentice the line trade is still worth learning if they also learn to test and question the machines. I wouldn't promise them a lifetime in a bucket truck.

say: I'd call for **careful equipment trials** before changing how crews repair lines.
I'd tell apprentices that **machine testing** belongs beside climbing skills.
think: At **40**, robot climbing may cut the pay attached to my lead role.
I think a **ten-year runway** could let me move into hardware trials.
do: Take the manufacturer's **robotic line equipment** course now.
Continue paid **field shifts** through 2037 and record trial failures.
Apply to **two nearby utilities** with the trial log while saving lead pay.
feel: **Calmer** with a decade, and sad about losing hands-on repairs.
S4.quote: I wouldn't promise them a lifetime in a bucket truck.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** supports a planned transition, while the loss of hands-on craft remains personal.
She names **test evidence** from old hardware and rain rather than assuming equipment demonstrations prove safety.

steps.text: Take the manufacturer course on robotic line equipment

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the office could change when I'm 29 and capable line robots could reach us when I'm 32. I'd want paid access to real equipment trials and a clear safety standard before any machine works beside a live crew. My savings give me choices, but they don't create a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who has the stop switch when a robot gets close to a live line. The ground crew must be able to stop it immediately, even if the plan came from a clever system miles away.

headlineQuote: My savings give me choices, but they don't create a job.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old lead** lineworker with a technical diploma, strong savings and several nearby utility employers.
She trusts **field judgment** and checks AI-produced records against her notebook before a crew acts.
Her concern rises when **2031 robots** could remove the climbing premium while she is still young.
With longer warning, she seeks **equipment trials** and keeps earning from field shifts while building options.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable robots could reach her crew when she is 32.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid equipment trials** and a clear safety standard before robots work beside live crews.
